slots.question: How long after the aqueous drug dilutions are made (at plate release) can they still be dispensed onto cells without loss of potency or precipitation?
slots.why: Drug_prep makes aqueous dilutions at plate release, and small molecules like sorafenib and erlotinib can precipitate or degrade in aqueous medium, so dispensing must happen soon after release.

No archive source gives a shorter precipitation or potency window, so the value is a maximum, not a recommended target. Review whether the lab wants a tighter default.

All four series are made in culture medium, not DMSO: a DMSO series would put about 8% DMSO into the top well, far above the 2% tolerance, while medium series keep worst-case well DMSO near 0.35%. Erlotinib and vinblastine get DMSO intermediates (1 mM erlotinib; 480, 48, 4.8 uM vinblastine) so every DMSO transfer is at least 9 ul (erlotinib) or 2.3 ul (vinblastine), inside the calibrated range; the MK-4827 (1.8 ul) and sorafenib (3.6 ul) direct stock transfers use the 50 ul tip in surface mode, which is calibrated down to 1 ul. Medium fill uses 300 ul surface (0.5 to 300 ul calibrated) for small volumes; the series 1/3 steps use jet on 300 ul tips (20 to 300 ul) so tips don't touch well contents. Batches are 100 ul per dilution-plate well and are remade at most every 1440 min (one day) because the aqueous dilutions are not to be stored beyond a day. Cell suspension: 9 plates per reservoir fill, 8 reservoirs in total, within the 20 on hand. Caveats: all powder is used exactly with no spare, and powder reorders take about two weeks, so any loss means a gap; intermediate DMSO dilutions were my choice and the calc does not model their solvent; the pipetting mode choices are my own within the catalog ranges.
